context: Current closing price of Microsoft (MSFT): $386.34 USD as of 2026-07-06.
justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish baseline for what appears to be an asset trading around the 388–390 range. For the one-day estimate of 388.5, I was essentially anchoring near the current price with minimal drift, reflecting the typical mean-reverting tendency of prices over very short horizons and the absence of any imminent scheduled catalysts that would strongly bias direction. For the one-week estimate of 391, I incorporated a slight upward drift, consistent with a modest positive expected return over that window while acknowledging that short-term momentum or macro sentiment could easily dominate. The one-month estimate of 396 extends that gentle upward slope, reflecting a longer-run drift assumption while remaining conservative — I did not want to project aggressive trend continuation without stronger fundamental justification.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to historical volatility patterns at each respective horizon. The one-day interval of roughly plus or minus 10.5 points reflects normal daily price fluctuation. The one-week interval widens to about plus or minus 21 points, scaling approximately with the square root of time as volatility compounds. The one-month interval of plus or minus 41 points follows that same logic but also incorporates additional uncertainty from macro developments, earnings cycles, and sentiment shifts that become more probable over a longer window. The asymmetry is relatively modest across all three horizons, suggesting I did not have strong skew priors in either direction at the time.

There are several tail risks that could push outcomes well outside these stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in macroeconomic data — such as a surprise in inflation readings, central bank policy shifts, or credit stress emerging in financial markets — could drive prices sharply lower, potentially breaching the lower bound of even the one-month interval. Geopolitical shocks or liquidity events are particularly dangerous because they tend to gap prices through support levels quickly. On the upside, a strong risk-on catalyst such as unexpectedly dovish central bank guidance, a major positive earnings surprise, or a resolution of an ongoing geopolitical uncertainty could push prices above the upper bound. These fat-tail events are by definition underweighted in standard confidence intervals, so real-world outcomes beyond my stated ranges should be considered genuinely plausible rather than negligible.
